source_read: PDF, Am J Epidemiol 179(7): 884–894 (all 11 pages, text layer read page by page); Table 5 and its text (p. 892), the Introduction (p. 884) and Results with Table 2 (p. 887) checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi

claims.overstatement: Table 5 lists the most commonly named substances for each code, not every substance. It does not show that all 2,725 T40.2 deaths named one of the six terms; other opioids coded T40.2 may account for some. The six counts overlap: they sum to 3,218, more than 2,725, because certificates often name several opioids. 'Whose certificates named oxycodone, …' and the magnitude's 'naming six terms' should read 'most often naming'.
claims.note: 2,725 and the six terms (oxycodone 1,047, morphine 648, hydrocodone 563, 'opiate' 543, hydromorphone 269, codeine 148) match Table 5 on the rendered page. 'Opiate' was counted only when no specific opiate was named, so 'just opiate' is accurate. Fentanyl and tramadol share T40.4 (521 deaths: fentanyl 198, tramadol 153, propoxyphene 141). Codes, and words, are what the certifier wrote: poisoning deaths of all intents, Washington residents, 2003–2010 (7,817). The paper does not say whether Table 5's code totals come from the official multiple-cause codes or from the author's own assignment of a code to each drug word (Methods, p. 886). Either way, the grouping the claim illustrates holds.

anchors.extracted: T40.2 'other opioids': 2,725 deaths. Most commonly named: oxycodone 1,047, morphine 648, hydrocodone 563, 'opiate' (counted only when no specific opiate was named) 543, hydromorphone 269, codeine 148. T40.4 'other synthetic narcotics': 521 deaths, mostly fentanyl 198, tramadol 153 and propoxyphene 141. By contrast, T40.1 is heroin only (539) and T40.3 methadone only (2,149).

Heroin (T40.1) and methadone (T40.3) have their own codes. Oxycodone, hydrocodone, morphine, 'opiates, not otherwise specified' and many other opiates all fall under T40.2. Fentanyl and tramadol go with other synthetic narcotics, and all benzodiazepines share one code. Two drugs with the same code written on the same certificate line get a single code.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; Results, paragraph on Table 5 (p. 890)
anchors.extracted: Of the 25 substances most often named, only 4 have a code that identifies them alone: methadone, alcohol, cocaine and heroin. The other 21 share codes and cannot be counted from ICD codes alone. The verbatim text (SuperMICAR) gives this detail.

Washington State resident deaths, 2003–2010, with a poisoning underlying cause (X40–X49, X60–X69, X85–X90, Y10–Y19), all intents, including non-drug poisonings. Deaths classed as drug or alcohol dependence, adverse effects of drugs in therapeutic use, and the 42 complications of medical care were excluded, leaving 7,817 (p. 886).

claims.note: The source shows both halves of the sentence. Text recovers names merged by codes: 21 of the top 25 substances have no unique code, and same-code drugs on one line collapse to a single code. Text cannot recover what was not written: its usefulness depends on how often certifiers name specific drugs (93% in Washington against 75% nationally, as cited), and 'opiate' alone cannot be resolved. The 93% and 75% are cited from another study (ref 28), not measured here. Text was not checked against toxicology or case files, and heroin versus morphine on certificates is flagged as uncertain.

anchors.extracted: By coding convention, a code is not repeated on the same certificate line, so 'fentanyl and tramadol' on one line yields one T40.4. The same drug on two lines is coded twice, so codes cannot show whether two codes mean two drugs or one drug written twice. The text gives the fuller picture of how many drugs were named.

Heroin and morphine counts are reported as written. Morphine found at autopsy may come from heroin, and certifiers' use of scene evidence may vary between counties or states. States differ in how fully drugs are specified: specific drugs were named on 93% of Washington drug-poisoning certificates in 2008–2010 against 75% nationally, and under 50% in some states (cited, ref 28). Text is less useful where few drugs are named.

anchors.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (starts on p. 886; the 'opiate' sentence is on p. 887); Results, 5th paragraph (p. 887) for the prescription/illicit shares
anchors.extracted: 'Opiate' appeared on 1,240 certificates (15.9%); 676 of these also named a specific opiate, so 564 named only 'opiate' (editors' calculation), a term the text cannot resolve. At least one prescription drug was named in 5,454 deaths (70%), at least one illicit drug in 2,162 (28%), and a term that could be either in a further 198 (3%).
21 of the 25 most often named substances cannot be identified or counted from ICD codes alone; the verbatim text identifies them.

key_findings.correction: Confirmed against the rotated Table 2 at 150 dpi: the ten pair counts and their ranking match.
Confirmed. Figure 4 at 300 dpi: the men's prescription-only line is above the women's in 7 of 8 years (2006 is the exception).

Confirmed. Two notes. Table 5 lists only the most commonly named substances per code; the six T40.2 counts overlap (sum 3,218 against 2,725 deaths), so they are not an exhaustive list. 'The author's assignment of codes to words' is the most plausible reading (T40.3 = methadone 2,149 and T40.1 = heroin 539 exactly), but the paper does not say so explicitly.

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed: 1,240 − 676 = 564 against 543 in Table 5 (T40.2 row) on the rendered pages.

risk_of_bias.note: I agree with JBI-prevalence, overall moderate. For what the claims use (which drugs share a code; that the text recovers merged names), risk is low. The prescription-versus-illicit comparison carries the moderate rating.

interpretation_gap.note: I agree with 'minor'. The conclusions are descriptive. The prescription-versus-illicit framing and 'involved' (meaning named) are the main gaps, and the card records them.

missed: The paper never gives its own count of the 7,817 deaths whose text named no specific drug, although Appendix Table 1 has a 'nonspecific' word category and Figures 4–5 show a 'neither' group only as rates. The only completeness figure (93% in 2008–2010 against 75% nationally) is cited from ref 28 (p. 892). This matters for the claim that text cannot recover a drug that was never written.

For the claim wording: Table 5's six T40.2 terms are the most commonly named, with overlapping counts (sum 3,218 > 2,725 deaths). The claim's 'whose certificates named [these six]' and the magnitude's 'naming six terms' read as exhaustive, which the table does not show.
